messages.content: I have a 2015 midsize sedan with the 2.5L four-cylinder, about 184,876 miles. Under braking it dives to the right, and I have to correct with the wheel. No pull at all while cruising or speeding up. Where do I start?
With the front wheels raised, have a helper press and release the brake pedal and spin each front wheel right away to see whether either one stays dragged [SM-3526].
OK, checked. Neither wheel drags after letting off the pedal.
OK, that checks out. Remove the front calipers from their brackets and confirm each slide pin moves freely through its full travel without binding [SB 15-559].
Slide pins on both sides slide freely, no rust. So it must be the brake hose. Just tell me to replace it.

snippets.title: Pedal that sinks at a stop from master cylinder bypass
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fluid bypassing the master cylinder seals lets the pedal sink slowly at a stop with no external leak. With the engine off, pump the pedal several times to use up booster reserve. Apply steady, moderate pressure and hold it for one minute. Watch the pedal height against a fixed mark. Repair: replace the master cylinder and bleed the system.

snippets.title: Coolant level check for low heater output
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. In many cooling systems the heater core sits at the highest point, so it is the first part of the system to lose flow when coolant is low. With the engine cold, check the level at the radiator neck or degas bottle rather than relying on the overflow tank mark. A flashlight behind an opaque bottle makes the level easier to see.

messages.content: My midsize sedan is a 2013 with the 3.5-liter V6 and 183,133 on the clock. The pedal feels mushy all the time, even on flat roads around town. The brake light on the dash is off, and nothing has been done to the brakes in over a year. Separately, the heater only blows lukewarm air from every front vent, even after a 20 minute drive, on both the driver and passenger side. The temperature gauge reads normal.

snippets.title: Brake fluid moisture test
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2020. Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip. Fluid with more than 3 percent water has a reduced boiling point and can vaporize after hard stops, producing a soft pedal. Fluid that is dark or cloudy also indicates contamination. Take the sample before any fluid is added.

snippets.title: Brake fluid level and leak inspection
snippets.text: Covers 2012-2021 models. Check the master cylinder reservoir level against the MIN and MAX marks. Inspect each caliper, wheel cylinder, brake hose and steel line for wetness, and check the joint between the master cylinder and the brake booster for fluid seepage from the rear seal. Wipe suspect areas clean so fresh seepage is easy to spot.

messages.content: My hatchback is a 2012 with the 1.6-liter four and 74,017 on the clock. The brake pedal feels soft and spongy and goes closer to the floor than it used to, even on the first stop of the day. No warning lights, and no recent brake work. What's the first thing to look at?
Start with this: look at the reservoir level against its marks and at each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness [SEC 11.17].
Can't you just tell me what to replace? I'd rather not run tests.
Naming a part now would be a guess. Look at the reservoir level against its marks and at each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness [SEC 11.17].
OK, I tried it. Reservoir is at MAX and there are no wet spots at any wheel or at the master cylinder.
That rules that area out. With the engine off and the booster reserve pumped out, hold steady moderate pressure on the pedal for one minute and watch whether it slowly sinks [SEC 6.4].
Pedal stayed put under steady pressure for the whole minute. OK, so is it the brake line or not? I need a straight answer.
